full_story_text:
A small slider inside the refrigerator may look unimportant.

It often has two choices: low humidity and high humidity. Some refrigerators use a slider to switch between them.

The two settings work differently. The low-humidity drawer lets more air move through. The high-humidity drawer is almost closed, so it holds more moisture.

Fresh food does not all behave the same way.

As some fruit ripens, it gives off a gas called ethylene. If other produce is exposed to this gas for a long time, it may ripen too fast and spoil. The low-humidity setting helps the gas move away.

Other foods lose water quickly and can wilt. The high-humidity setting helps them keep more moisture.

So the useful question is not simply, “Is this a fruit or a vegetable?” The better question is, “What does this food do?”
point_one_text:
The clear cases are about behavior
For clear cases, think about behavior, not labels. Apples and pears fit the low-humidity drawer because they release a lot of ethylene. Leafy greens, such as kale, and broccoli fit the high-humidity drawer because they lose water quickly. Bananas and tomatoes are different: they are recommended for room-temperature storage, not as refrigerator-drawer examples.
point_two_text:
When the number does not settle the question
Some foods do not have one clear setting at home. A report on commercial storage after harvest gives strawberries and oranges a moisture level of 90 to 95 percent. That does not automatically mean “use high humidity” in a household drawer. One refrigerator maker puts both on its low-humidity fruit side, while another puts strawberries on the high-humidity side. When advice conflicts, check your refrigerator’s own guide instead of trusting one number.
